claims.text: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 is a eutectic alloy containing FCC/B2 lamellae.
Cryogenic rolling followed by warm rolling and a short anneal near 700 °C will refine the alloy's lamellar microstructure.
The proposed processing sequence will increase heterogeneous-interface density and produce partially recrystallized ultrafine features.
Cryo-rolling and annealing can create a hierarchical microstructure containing ultrafine, recovered, partially recrystallized, and coarse constituents in AlCoCrFeNi2.1.
A refined lamellar structure and heterogeneous interfaces promote enhanced strain hardening.
A refined lamellar structure and increased heterogeneous-interface density improve crack-arrest capability.
The hierarchical microstructure produced by cryogenic deformation and annealing can improve strength and ductility simultaneously in AlCoCrFeNi2.1.
The full cryogenic-then-warm rolling and 700 °C annealing sequence will increase yield strength by at least 30% relative to the as-cast alloy.
The full processing sequence will preserve or moderately increase ductility relative to the as-cast alloy.
The cryogenic rolling step should be conducted at −196 °C.
The intermediate warm-rolling step should be conducted at approximately 400 °C.
Annealing at 700 °C for approximately 15–30 minutes is an effective final treatment for the proposed processing sequence.
Adequate cryogenic rolling strain is required for the strength–ductility improvement.
Warm rolling must remain below the full-recrystallization threshold to preserve the proposed benefit.
A short anneal is required to avoid excessive grain growth, whereas an overly long anneal may reduce the synergy and degrade ductility.
The exact mechanical-property gains depend on rolling reductions and annealing hold times.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis says both strength and ductility will be increased, but the predicted outcome and falsification rule permit unchanged ductility. Thus, a result with increased strength but merely equal ductility would satisfy the stated test while not demonstrating the claimed increase in both properties.

The predicted outcome requires at least a 30% yield-strength increase, whereas the falsification rule requires only an unspecified increase. A gain below 30% could therefore pass the experiment's rule despite failing the quantitative prediction.
